title: GCD & LCM
coreInsight: Prime factorization lets us compare multiplicative structure: the GCD keeps the prime powers shared by both numbers, while the LCM contains every prime power required by either.
targetLearnerRealization: GCD is the prime structure two numbers share, while LCM is the smallest prime inventory sufficient to build both numbers.
learningObjectives: Build the GCD from the shared copies in two prime factorizations.
Build the LCM from enough copies to reconstruct either number.
Distinguish common factors from common multiples and choose the operation a situation requires.
Retain prime multiplicities by using smaller exponents for GCD and larger exponents for LCM.

continuity.openingCallback: Line up the prime-factor inventories of 24 and 36 to compare shared and sufficient collections.
closingSeeds: Shared-factor and common-cycle reasoning can simplify later divisibility and remainder problems.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: GCD and LCM are easily swapped.
The LCM always equals the product of the two numbers.
Common factors and common multiples are the same kind of object.

beats.purpose: Create the shared-versus-sufficient distinction before naming GCD and LCM.
beats.expectedRealization: For 24 and 36, the largest shared prime inventory is 2² × 3 = 12, while the smallest inventory able to build either is 2³ × 3² = 72.
beats.transitionIn: The prime tiles for 24 and 36 are already lined up. Now build two different trays: what both can share, and what is enough to build either one.
beats.transitionOut: The shared tray used the shorter stack in each prime column; the sufficient tray used the taller stack.
beats.whyNow: A concrete inventory choice gives GCD and LCM distinct meanings before their names appear.
beats.entryBridge: Use 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3². Compare one prime column at a time.
beats.exitBridge: The products 12 and 72 pass opposite reconstruction checks.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Aligned prime-factor tiles organized by prime and multiplicity.
learnerPrompts: How many 2-tiles and 3-tiles can both numbers supply?
How many of each tile are needed to build either number?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the largest shared product is 12 and the smallest sufficient product is 72.
beats.incorrectFeedback: In each prime column, use the smaller count for what both share and the larger count for what can build either.

visual.ariaLabel: Prime tiles for twenty-four and thirty-six compared in shared and sufficient trays

steps.body: Both inventories contain two 2s and one 3, whose product is 12.
To contain either inventory, keep three 2s and two 3s, whose product is 72.

resolution.takeaway: Shared uses what both contain; sufficient uses everything either one requires.

beats.purpose: Generalize the shared tray to the smaller exponent rule.
beats.expectedRealization: A factor common to both numbers cannot use more copies of a prime than either number contains.
beats.transitionIn: Focus only on the tray that must divide both 24 and 36.
beats.prompt: For a prime appearing with exponents 3 and 2, which exponent belongs in the greatest shared factor?

options.text: 2, because both inventories contain at least two copies.
3, because greatest always means the larger exponent.
5, because the exponents should be added.
0, because the exponents differ.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—the shared collection cannot exceed the shorter stack.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A common factor must be buildable from each number's inventory separately.

steps.body: Both numbers can supply two copies. Only one can supply a third, so the shared exponent is min(3,2) = 2.

resolution.takeaway: For each prime, the greatest shared factor uses the smaller exponent.

beats.purpose: Generalize the sufficient tray to the larger exponent rule.
beats.expectedRealization: A multiple of both numbers must contain at least every prime copy required by either.
beats.transitionIn: Now switch the requirement: one tray must contain enough tiles to reconstruct either number.
beats.prompt: For a prime appearing with exponents 1 and 4, which exponent belongs in the smallest sufficient multiple?

options.text: 4, because the tray must meet the larger requirement.
1, because least always means the smaller exponent.
5, because every copy must be duplicated.
3, because the exponents should be subtracted.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—the taller requirement must fit, and adding extra copies would not be least.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask how many copies are necessary to reconstruct the number that needs four.

steps.body: Four copies are necessary to build the second number and are also enough for the first. Thus max(1,4) = 4.

resolution.takeaway: For each prime, the smallest sufficient multiple uses the larger exponent.

beats.purpose: Name both operations after their opposing inventory roles are established.
beats.expectedRealization: GCD/GCF is the greatest shared divisor; LCM is the least shared multiple.
beats.transitionIn: The two trays answer two different comparison questions and need distinct names.
beats.name: Greatest common divisor and least common multiple
beats.conciseDefinition: The GCD (also called GCF) is the greatest positive integer dividing both numbers; the LCM is the least positive integer divisible by both.
beats.formalization: If a = ∏pᵅ and b = ∏pᵝ, then GCD uses p^min(ᵅ,ᵝ) and LCM uses p^max(ᵅ,ᵝ).
beats.memoryHook: GCD shares the shorter stacks; LCM covers the taller stacks.

beats.purpose: Separate common-factor situations from common-multiple situations.
beats.expectedRealization: Equal largest group size asks for a common factor; first synchronized repeat asks for a common multiple.
beats.transitionIn: Choose the operation from what the unknown represents, not from whichever acronym appears familiar.

options.text: Largest equal group size → GCD; first time two cycles meet → LCM.
Largest equal group size → LCM; first time two cycles meet → GCD.
Both situations always ask for GCD.
Both situations always ask for the product.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct—group size must divide both totals, while a meeting time must be a multiple of both periods.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask whether the unknown divides both given numbers or is divisible by both given numbers.

steps.body: A group size is a factor of each total, so maximize among common factors.
A meeting time contains whole cycles of each period, so minimize among positive common multiples.

resolution.takeaway: Factors divide the inputs; multiples are divisible by the inputs.

beats.purpose: Show why multiplying the inputs can overcount shared prime structure.
beats.expectedRealization: When inputs share prime factors, their product contains duplicate shared copies beyond what the LCM needs.
beats.transitionIn: The product is always a common multiple, but it may carry unnecessary duplicate tiles.
beats.prompt: Why is LCM(18, 24) equal to 72 instead of 18 × 24 = 432?

options.text: The product counts the shared factor 6 twice; 72 already contains enough prime copies for both numbers.
The LCM is always the smaller input.
A common multiple must divide both inputs.
Eighteen is not prime.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—72 = 2³ × 3² contains the maximum required exponents and no extra copies.

steps.body: Use max exponents: 2³ × 3² = 72. Both 18 and 24 divide 72.
The product 432 = 2⁴ × 3³ duplicates the shared 2 × 3 and is a common multiple, but not the least one.

resolution.takeaway: The LCM equals the product only when the inputs share no prime factor.

beats.purpose: Use divisibility checks to keep GCD and LCM directions straight.
beats.expectedRealization: The GCD divides each input, while each input divides the LCM.
beats.transitionIn: Before using the trays in a contest problem, turn their meanings into a quick directional check.
beats.prompt: For 24 and 36, which pair of checks is correct?

options.text: 12 divides both 24 and 36; both 24 and 36 divide 72.
24 and 36 divide 12; 72 divides both 24 and 36.
Both 12 and 72 must divide the inputs.
Divisibility cannot check GCD or LCM.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—the arrows point inward for GCD and outward toward LCM.
beats.incorrectFeedback: GCD is a factor of each input; LCM is a multiple of each input.

resolution.takeaway: GCD divides both; LCM is divisible by both.

beats.purpose: Build a three-number LCM and use it as a step size inside an interval.
beats.expectedRealization: The maximum prime stacks give LCM 300, and its three multiples strictly between 1000 and 2000 are 1200, 1500, and 1800.
beats.transitionIn: Three divisibility requirements now feed one sufficient tray, then that tray becomes a repeating step along an interval.
beats.transitionOut: The tray value 300 generated exactly three qualifying integers in the interval.
beats.whyNow: The approved problem makes LCM the minimal sufficient prime inventory and then uses its multiples for a complete count.
beats.entryBridge: Factor 15, 20, and 25; retain the tallest stack of each prime; then list multiples in the stated range.
beats.exitBridge: The interval endpoints exclude 900 and 2100, leaving three internal stamps.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Color-coded prime stacks merged by coordinate-wise maxima.
learnerPrompts: Which prime powers must every qualifying number contain?
Why is 300 the smallest sufficient product?
Which multiples of 300 lie strictly between the endpoints?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—1200, 1500, and 1800 are the three qualifying integers.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Find LCM(15,20,25) from maximum prime exponents, then enumerate its multiples between 1000 and 2000.

steps.body: The sufficient inventory is 2² × 3 × 5² = 300.
The multiples of 300 strictly between 1000 and 2000 are 1200, 1500, and 1800, so the count is 3.

resolution.takeaway: After finding an LCM, its multiples enumerate every simultaneous divisibility solution.

beats.purpose: Expose the error of keeping only distinct shared primes.
beats.expectedRealization: GCD(24,40) contains three shared copies of 2, so it is 8 rather than 2.
beats.transitionIn: A prime appearing in both numbers may be shared more than once; the stack height matters.
beats.prompt: Given 24 = 2³ × 3 and 40 = 2³ × 5, what is their GCD?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—both inventories share all three copies of 2, giving 2³ = 8.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use the smaller exponent in the 2-column: min(3,3) = 3.

visual.ariaLabel: Three shared copies of two in twenty-four and forty

resolution.takeaway: Prime identity and prime multiplicity both matter.

beats.purpose: Compute GCF and LCM from the same prime inventories and compare them by ratio.
beats.expectedRealization: Minimum exponents give GCF 18, maximum exponents give LCM 5940, and the ratio is 330.
beats.transitionIn: One pair of inventories now feeds both trays; keep min and max exponent choices distinct through the final ratio.
beats.transitionOut: The overlap produced 18, the union produced 5940, and 5940 ÷ 18 = 330.
beats.whyNow: The approved transfer forces both operations from the same factorizations, making a swap or lost multiplicity immediately visible.
beats.entryBridge: Factor each number, place shared copies in the overlap, and retain all copies needed by either number for the LCM.
beats.exitBridge: Dividing the full sufficient inventory by the shared inventory leaves the nonshared prime structure.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Prime-factor tiles split into shared overlap and number-specific regions.
learnerPrompts: Which prime copies belong in the overlap?
Which copies are required across the full union?
What ratio does the problem request?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use 180 = 2² × 3² × 5 and 594 = 2 × 3³ × 11. Take minimum exponents for GCF and maximum exponents for LCM.

steps.body: Minimum exponents give GCF = 2 × 3² = 18. Maximum exponents give LCM = 2² × 3³ × 5 × 11 = 5940.
The requested ratio is 5940 ÷ 18 = 330.

resolution.takeaway: The same aligned inventories support both operations: minimum for GCD, maximum for LCM.

beats.purpose: Assess GCD by shared prime inventory.
beats.transitionIn: Build only the largest tray that can divide both inputs.
beats.transitionOut: The shared inventory 2² × 3 reconstructs 12 and divides both numbers.
beats.whyNow: A near item isolates GCD selection.
beats.exitBridge: Choose minimum exponents in every column.
learnerPrompts: Which prime copies occur in both?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Take 2² and 3¹, the shorter shared stacks.

steps.body: Minimum exponents give 2² × 3 = 12. Both 48 and 60 divide evenly by 12.

resolution.takeaway: GCD is the product of the shared minimum prime powers.

beats.purpose: Assess LCM by sufficient prime inventory.
beats.transitionIn: Now build the smallest tray able to reconstruct either input.
beats.whyNow: A near item isolates LCM selection.
beats.exitBridge: Choose maximum exponents and verify both inputs divide the result.
learnerPrompts: Which taller prime stacks are required?
Is the result divisible by both inputs?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use two copies each of 2 and 3.

steps.body: Maximum exponents give 2² × 3² = 36. Dividing by 12 gives 3 and dividing by 18 gives 2.

resolution.takeaway: LCM is the product of the sufficient maximum prime powers.

beats.purpose: Assess simultaneous GCD and LCM calculation.
beats.expectedRealization: For 45 and 60, minimum exponents give 15 and maximum exponents give 180.
beats.transitionIn: Use one alignment to build both trays without swapping them.
beats.transitionOut: The shared result 15 divides inward; the sufficient result 180 is divisible outward.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item coordinates both operations.
learnerPrompts: What do the minimum exponents produce?
What do the maximum exponents produce?

steps.body: The shared inventory is 3 × 5 = 15. The sufficient inventory is 2² × 3² × 5 = 180.

resolution.takeaway: Minimum and maximum exponent trays can be built from one alignment.

beats.purpose: Assess operation choice in a repeating-cycle context.
beats.expectedRealization: The first positive time divisible by both 8 and 12 is their LCM, 24.
beats.transitionIn: Translate a synchronized repeat into a common-multiple question.
beats.transitionOut: Twenty-four minutes contains three 8-minute cycles and two 12-minute cycles.
beats.whyNow: A mixed context checks meaning beyond explicit operation vocabulary.
beats.entryBridge: The meeting time must be divisible by each period.
beats.exitBridge: Use the least positive common multiple, not the greatest common divisor.
learnerPrompts: Must the answer divide the periods or contain whole periods?
What is the first common multiple?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the signals align again after 24 minutes.
beats.incorrectFeedback: List multiples of 8 and 12 until the first match.

steps.body: Multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, …; multiples of 12 are 12, 24, …. The first positive match is 24.

resolution.takeaway: First synchronized repetition calls for an LCM.

beats.purpose: Assess LCM generation plus a strict lower bound.
beats.expectedRealization: Common multiples of 18 and 24 are multiples of 72; the least one greater than 100 is 144.
beats.transitionIn: For the final challenge, combine the sufficient tray with an interval boundary.
beats.transitionOut: The base step is 72; its first multiple above 100 is 144.
beats.whyNow: The challenge composes LCM structure with ordered enumeration.
beats.entryBridge: Find the LCM first, then inspect its multiples around 100.
beats.exitBridge: Seventy-two is too small; twice 72 is the first qualifying value.
learnerPrompts: What is the least common step size?
beats.incorrectFeedback: LCM(18,24) = 72. List 72, 144, … and apply the strict bound.

steps.body: 18 = 2 × 3² and 24 = 2³ × 3, so their LCM is 2³ × 3² = 72.
The multiples begin 72, 144, 216. The first one greater than 100 is 144.

resolution.takeaway: Once the LCM is known, all common multiples are its multiples.

beats.purpose: Consolidate operation choice, exponent rules, and directional checks.
beats.expectedRealization: GCD and LCM are paired but opposite inventory constructions.
beats.transitionIn: Every example can now be checked by the same four-part comparison.
beats.prompt: Which statements belong in a reliable GCD/LCM comparison? Select all four.

options.text: GCD uses the smaller exponent in each prime column.
LCM uses the larger exponent in each prime column.
GCD divides both inputs; both inputs divide the LCM.
Grouping size suggests GCD; synchronized cycles suggest LCM.
LCM must always equal the product of the inputs.

response.feedback: Keep the min/max rules, direction check, and situation meaning together.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—those four statements distinguish and verify the operations.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A shared factor can make the raw product larger than the least common multiple.

resolution.takeaway: GCD keeps shared minimum stacks; LCM keeps sufficient maximum stacks.

beats.purpose: Connect the completed lesson to broader number-theory modeling.
beats.expectedRealization: Prime inventories turn grouping and repetition questions into explicit structural comparisons.
beats.transitionIn: A factor question looks inward at what two numbers contain; a cycle question looks outward at when their repetitions meet.
beats.prompt: When a new problem describes equal groups or repeating cycles without naming an operation, what divisibility direction will tell you whether to build the shared tray or the sufficient tray?
beats.takeaway: Translate the situation into who divides whom; the correct prime-inventory construction follows.

notes: Draft foundation lesson authored from the approved N3 compact context packet.
Shared and sufficient prime trays establish the smaller/larger exponent rules before GCD and LCM are named.
Both approved AMC problems are integrated in their mapped roles with whole-scene animations.
All four mapped misconceptions are explicitly repaired through operation-choice, product-overcount, direction, and multiplicity tasks.
All generated answers were independently checked by prime-exponent comparison and a separate division, enumeration, or reconstruction method.
No lesson-specific renderer infrastructure was added.
